headline: A Free, Local AI Pipeline Designed for Working VFX Artists
lede: Most AI video tools treat professional VFX artists as an afterthought — the outputs are pretty but uncontrollable, the pipelines are cloud-locked, and the results rarely survive contact with a real compositing suite. A new free workflow built by @mickmumpitz, demonstrated in a 2026 masterclass, aims to change that by integrating local AI video generation directly into a node-based ComfyUI setup. The pitch is control: artists drive the tool rather than prompting into a black box.
body:
**ComfyUI** is a free, open-source interface for running Stable Diffusion models that organises operations as a visual graph of connected nodes — closer in spirit to a compositing application like Nuke than to a consumer image generator. Because it runs locally, it keeps footage and assets off third-party servers and imposes no usage caps, which matters when client NDAs or bandwidth constraints are involved.

The workflow demonstrated in the tutorial extends ComfyUI beyond still-image generation into video, a substantially harder problem. AI video generation is computationally expensive and prone to temporal flickering — the model has no innate understanding that frame 47 should look like frame 46. Production-ready pipelines must account for this through techniques like optical-flow warping, temporal attention conditioning, or frame-by-frame guidance from reference imagery.

The tutorial draws on the same family of tools that ActionVFX's course covers for VFX image work: *ControlNet* (a technique that conditions generation on structural cues such as depth maps or edge detection), *LoRAs* (Low-Rank Adaptation — small, composable model fine-tunes that steer style or subject without retraining the whole model), and *IP Adapters* (Image Prompt Adapters, which let a reference image guide generation rather than relying solely on text). Together these give an artist levers that a simple text-prompt interface does not.

The output side matters as much as the generation side for professional work. VFX pipelines do not consume flattened video; they consume layered *EXR* files (the OpenEXR format, the industry standard for high-dynamic-range, multi-channel image sequences) that preserve depth, alpha, and lighting passes separately. The ActionVFX course, which targets similar ground, explicitly covers exporting EXRs ready for Nuke, After Effects, or DaVinci Resolve — suggesting the broader ecosystem is converging on this integration point.

Running everything locally has a real cost: consumer hardware capable of generating video at useful resolutions (a high-VRAM GPU, typically 16 GB or more) is not cheap. But for studios already equipped for on-premise rendering, the absence of per-frame cloud fees and the ability to iterate without internet latency represents a meaningful operational shift. The broader signal is that the tools for professional AI-assisted VFX are maturing past the hobbyist proof-of-concept stage.

concepts.definition: A free, open-source graphical interface for running Stable Diffusion image and video models locally. Operations are arranged as a node graph — similar to a visual effects compositing application — which lets users build reproducible, inspectable workflows rather than relying on a single prompt box.

A neural network extension for Stable Diffusion that conditions image generation on structural inputs such as depth maps, edge-detection outlines, or pose skeletons. It gives artists spatial control over where objects appear and how the scene is structured, rather than leaving layout entirely to chance.

Low-Rank Adaptation — a technique for fine-tuning a large AI model by training only a small set of additional weight adjustments. LoRAs are compact files that can be layered onto a base model to steer its style or subject matter without the cost of full retraining.

Image Prompt Adapter — a module that lets a reference photograph or frame guide AI image generation alongside (or instead of) a text prompt. Useful in VFX when the artist has a specific look or subject to match rather than a verbal description.

The industry-standard file format for visual effects image sequences. EXR files store high-dynamic-range data and support multiple channels in a single file — colour, depth, alpha, lighting passes — so compositors can manipulate layers independently in applications like Nuke or After Effects.
